idiom_name: pure functions returning values, std::optional/std::variant outcomes, [[nodiscard]]
implementation_notes: Make the core free functions that take inputs by value or `const&` and return the result by value - a plain `struct`, `std::optional` for 'nothing', `std::variant<...>` when the outcome is one of several shapes, `[[nodiscard]]` so ignoring a decision warns - and keep IO out: no `iostream`, no `<filesystem>`, no clock. The classic OO form (a Core class with injected port interfaces) is only justified where the decision must describe an effect rather than compute one; then return the step as a value and let the shell perform it. On a C++23 toolchain `std::expected<T, E>` replaces hand-rolled public/protected member + optional error plumbing and composes the fallible steps with `and_then`/`transform`.
pitfalls: Returning a reference, `std::string_view` or pointer into a function-local value from the core dangles - the core must return owning values, and `const&` parameters do not license `const_cast`.
A `const` member function can still mutate `mutable` members or the pointee behind a `shared_ptr` it holds, so constness is not purity: an injected cache or a `std::function` that logs is an effect.
`std::expected`/`std::optional` are not silently checked: an ignored return value is a dropped decision, so annotate them `[[nodiscard]]` (the standard does not).

variants.name: Compile-time decision core (C++20)
variants.idiom_name: consteval/constexpr rule functions evaluated while compiling
variants.implementation_notes: C++20 lets the core itself be evaluated at compile time: declare rule functions `constexpr`, and the ones that must never run at runtime `consteval`. A compile-time evaluation cannot open a file, read the clock or allocate unboundedly, so the compiler itself proves the function is pure - the strongest enforcement this pattern gets in any of these languages. The shell then holds no decision code at all: the answer was folded into a constant (or a `static_assert`). Use it for policy tables, protocol mappings, dimension and unit conversions, and validation of literal configuration; decisions that depend on runtime values stay in the stage-1 value-semantics functions, because only constexpr inputs can be folded.
pitfalls: A `consteval` function called with a runtime value is a hard compile error, so a rule needed on runtime input must be `constexpr` instead - and a `constexpr` function is only *proven* pure on the paths the compiler actually evaluates.

Constant-evaluation failures surface as long, cascading diagnostics at the call site, not at the offending line; guard runtime escapes with `std::is_constant_evaluated()` and keep evaluation budgets in mind.
The compile-time core tempts you to encode mutable global configuration as constants, which freezes policy into the binary and forces a rebuild for what should be data.
